record.title: Discovery Foundation Models proposes explicit research-state revision with gated external evidence
record.summary: Yang, Yin and Wu define Discovery Foundation Models (DFMs) as systems that can find research questions, revise representations and hypotheses, select interventions, update from external evidence and improve across tasks. Their Zetema design keeps problems, hypotheses, evidence, interventions and budgets explicit and gates consequential actions. The paper proposes training and process-centered evaluation; its project repository describes Zetema as a research design whose implementation and validation progress remain future work. It also describes GALILEO as a real therapeutic-peptide discovery loop in which wet-lab outcomes changed later decisions across five optimization rounds. The cited GALILEO primary paper was not accessible in this review, and this case does not establish general-purpose DFM capability.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors define a DFM framework with seven coupled capabilities and describe Zetema as a system design with explicit research-state objects, external evidence, action gating and validated cross-task skill updates.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper describes GALILEO as a therapeutic-peptide wet-lab discovery loop in which biological measurements changed target beliefs, assay choices, mechanism hypotheses and later peptide designs; the authors report two organoid branches with IC50 values of 18.922 μM and 0.736 μM and consolidation of a reusable Amphiphilic Balance Grammar across five optimization rounds.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The linked project README describes Zetema as a research design and states that implementation and validation progress will be reported through linked projects; this review did not establish a released Zetema implementation.

claims.label: SPECULATIVE
claims.text: The framework and GALILEO case establish a validated general-purpose DFM with cross-domain transferable discovery skills.

contradictory_evidence: The paper states that GALILEO should not be interpreted as solving the general-purpose DFM problem: its domain, molecular modality, interfaces and objectives remain structured, and broader cross-domain transfer is open.
The linked project repository calls Zetema a research design and says implementation and validation progress will be reported through later project releases.
The cited primary GALILEO study could not be fetched in this review; its therapeutic measurements and five-round transfer description are secondary claims here.

evidence_gaps.description: The framework paper summarizes the GALILEO physical case, but the cited primary DOI redirected to a bioRxiv page that returned HTTP 500 through the available browser tool. The reported measurements and five-round design-rule transfer were not independently checked against that study.
The proposed general DFM training and evaluation program is not demonstrated by a validated Zetema implementation or cross-domain transfer results in the inspected sources.

brief.importance_rationale: If systems can identify and reformulate research questions, select informative interventions, revise from external results and transfer validated operations, they could change how scientific discovery systems are built and evaluated. A 5 reflects an influential framework and a reported domain-specific physical case, while general DFM capability, released Zetema implementation and cross-domain transfer remain unvalidated.
limitations: The seven-capability DFM framework and Zetema training/evaluation methods are proposals, not a demonstrated general-purpose discovery system.
The GALILEO case is a structured therapeutic-peptide workflow; its generalization across scientific domains is not established.
This review inspected the framework paper’s summary of GALILEO but not the cited primary paper; the reported measurements and transfer claims remain unchecked here.
The described physical loop includes human-executed specialist assays and human scientific judgment; consequential work is not attributed to an autonomous model alone.
No independent evaluation of reusable discovery-skill transfer, resource-matched performance or general DFM capability was established.
brief.summary: Yang, Yin and Wu define Discovery Foundation Models (DFMs) as systems that can find research questions, revise representations and hypotheses, select interventions, update from external evidence and improve across tasks. Their Zetema design keeps problems, hypotheses, evidence, interventions and budgets explicit and gates consequential actions. The paper proposes training and process-centered evaluation; its project repository describes Zetema as a research design whose implementation and validation progress remain future work. It also describes GALILEO as a real therapeutic-peptide discovery loop in which wet-lab outcomes changed later decisions across five optimization rounds. The cited GALILEO primary paper was not accessible in this review, and this case does not establish general-purpose DFM capability.

technical.claimed_result: The DFM paper reports a GALILEO therapeutic-peptide case in which physical outcomes changed later target beliefs, assay selection, mechanisms and design policy. It reports organoid IC50 measurements of 18.922 μM and 0.736 μM on two branches and five wet-lab optimization rounds culminating in the Amphiphilic Balance Grammar. The cited primary study was inaccessible in this review.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected paper defines a seven-capability framework and specifies Zetema architecture, training objectives and process-centered evaluation. It does not establish that the general DFM capability has been implemented or validated.
technical.implementation_status: The project repository describes Zetema as a research design; no released Zetema implementation was identified. It links separate projects including ScienceBuddy, ScienceIDE and JEPA-Anything.
technical.mechanism: Zetema is proposed as a model-system design that tracks problems, representations, hypotheses, evidence, interventions, resource/risk budgets and memory as linked research-state objects. A research world model predicts outcomes and costs; action-specific verifiers gate costly or consequential steps; external observations update the state; candidate discovery skills transfer only after held-out or shadow-mode validation.
technical.regime: Conceptual framework for digital, simulated, embodied and physical discovery systems. Empirical grounding is a paper-described structured therapeutic-peptide case with robotic synthesis and phenotyping plus human-executed specialized assays; broader transfer is untested.
technical.reproducibility: The DFM framework is a proposal and was not independently implemented or tested. The secondary GALILEO description cites a primary study that could not be fetched; the case and reported transfer were not independently reproduced here.
technical.strongest_baseline: No matched evaluation establishes the proposed framework’s performance over existing scientific agents. The paper proposes resource-matched, process-centered controls but reports no general DFM benchmark result.

brief.title: Discovery Foundation Models proposes explicit research-state revision with gated external evidence
brief.why_it_matters: The framework makes testable what an open-ended discovery claim would need to show: evidence must revise the research state and later decisions, while cross-task skills require held-out validation. The GALILEO case, as summarized by the authors, illustrates a domain-specific physical feedback loop; the general DFM architecture, training recipe and transfer claim remain proposals without a validated Zetema implementation in the inspected sources.
